summary: Proposes experimental extensions to TCP so it can use fast, long-delay network paths efficiently, where the original header limits made it hard to keep the pipe full. It is an Experimental document that asked for discussion, and it was replaced by RFC 1323.

plainLanguage.summary: A long, fat water pipe only works well if you keep pouring in lots of water at once. This fixes a rule that limited how much could be poured.

questions: how can tcp work better on high speed paths
what tcp extensions did rfc 1185 propose
why does tcp need timestamps on high speed networks
what is the bandwidth delay product
how does tcp handle old duplicate segments
what is a long fat network
subtitle: Extensions to TCP so it can reliably send data at gigabit speeds over long-distance paths.

tldr.problem: As fiber optics enabled faster networks, TCP's 32-bit sequence number space could wrap around (cycle) while segments were still in flight, risking data corruption. Existing TCP assumptions about segment lifetime no longer held.
tldr.mechanism: TCP can include timestamps in data segments via the Echo option; the receiver rejects segments with timestamps older than recently accepted in-sequence segments, preventing old duplicates from being mistaken for new data.
tldr.outcome: This experimental RFC proposed a practical solution using existing options, and it was succeeded by RFC 1323, which was in turn superseded by later TCP extensions.

today: RFC 1185 is Experimental and was superseded by RFC 1323. Modern TCP implementations widely support timestamps, and the feature is essential for reliable high-speed operation.

sections.title: The Problem: Sequence Wrap-Around at High Speeds
sections.content:
TCP uses a 32-bit sequence number field. At higher transmission speeds, the entire sequence space (2^31 bytes) can cycle and reuse sequence numbers faster than the maximum segment lifetime (MSL) allows old segments to expire from the network. This creates a reliability hazard: an old segment from an earlier transmission could arrive at the receiver just as its sequence number has wrapped around and lands in the current receive window.

The problem depends on the bandwidth*delay product: the product of the transfer rate in bytes per second and the round-trip delay in seconds. This product measures how much data "fills the pipe". For a 1 Mbps link with a 100 ms round-trip delay, the product is 12.5 KB; at 100 Mbps over a transcontinental 60 ms RTT, it is 750 KB. Modern gigabit speeds make this problem acute: at 1 Gbps, the sequence space cycles in just 17 seconds, well below typical MSL values.
sections.plainLanguage: If you pour water down a garden hose very, very fast, by the time you fill it the water from the beginning is still partway down. If you use the same pressure numbers twice (wrap around), the old water and new water get mixed up.

sections.title: TCP Timestamps as a Solution
sections.content:
RFC 1072 defined two TCP options called Echo and Echo Reply, which can carry 32-bit timestamps. When a TCP sender includes an Echo option with its current timestamp in a data segment, the receiver echoes that same timestamp back in its acknowledgment. The sender uses this to measure the round-trip time accurately—a benefit on long-delay networks where sampling rate becomes important.

The same timestamps also solve the sequence wrap-around problem. The receiver can reject any segment whose timestamp is earlier than the timestamp of the most recently accepted in-sequence segment. Since old duplicates carry old timestamps, they are discarded. The timestamp acts as a logical extension of the sequence number: even if the 32-bit sequence field has wrapped around, the timestamp distinguishes new data from old.

Crucially, the timestamp does not need to be synchronized with the receiver's clock; it is treated simply as a monotone-increasing serial number. A 1 ms timestamp clock can provide protection up to link speeds of 2 Gbps, and a 1 second clock works reliably up to gigabit speeds.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package gets a date stamp. When one arrives, you check the date and throw it away if it is too old for the current time. Old water in the hose has an old date, so you know to ignore it.

sections.title: Handling Old Duplicates from Earlier Connections
sections.content:
A second threat comes when a connection closes and immediately reopens using the same socket pair. An old segment from the closed connection could still be in transit and arrive at the wrong moment, falling within the window of the new incarnation and corrupting data.

TCP currently handles this with two mechanisms: TIME-WAIT state, which holds a closed socket for 2*MSL (4 minutes) after the final close handshake, and a quiet time of one MSL at system startup (to handle segments left over from a crash). If timestamps are used, a simpler approach becomes possible: the receiver can cache the latest timestamp from each remote host and reject any segment with a timestamp older than that cached value, even if the connection is new.

If the timestamp clock can be guaranteed monotonic across system crashes (for example, by synchronizing the clock at startup and ensuring boot takes longer than one clock tick), the quiet time becomes unnecessary. The TIME-WAIT delay is still needed for the TCP close handshake to complete reliably, but only for ~1 minute, not the full 4 minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: When you close a connection and open a new one with the same address, old segments from the old connection might still arrive. With timestamps, the receiver remembers "the highest timestamp I saw from this address was X" and throws away anything older than that.

sections.title: Implementation and Performance
sections.content:
The timestamp check is relatively expensive (interval arithmetic on a 32-bit field). On high-speed links, checking every segment could slow performance. The RFC suggests that implementations can optimize by performing "header prediction" first (a fast check to see if the segment is the expected next one) and only running the expensive timestamp check if header prediction fails. Analysis shows the probability of a false positive (an old duplicate accidentally matching the predicted sequence number) is negligibly small compared to the TCP checksum's own unreliability.

The timestamp option adds 12 bytes per segment (the option header plus the 4-byte timestamp value and 4-byte echo reply slot). For large transfers, this overhead is typically less than 0.5 percent.
sections.plainLanguage: The date-stamp check takes a little time. Smart receivers can skip it for most packets (the ones they were expecting) and only check old ones. It is worth the tiny slowdown to avoid data corruption.

sections.title: Scope and Limitations
sections.content:
This RFC focuses narrowly on solving the sequence wrap-around problem at high speeds using timestamps via an existing option mechanism (RFC 1072). It addresses two specific failure modes: wrap-around within the same connection, and old segments from earlier incarnations.

The solution does not address all of TCP's assumptions about network behavior. For example, it assumes the timestamp clock can tick at least once per MSL. It also assumes that if timestamps are used universally, MSL enforcement by the Internet layer (TTL) becomes unnecessary—but adoption remains incomplete, so the quiet time and TIME-WAIT delay are still practical safeguards.

The RFC notes that truly "long fat networks" (high bandwidth and long delay) also need larger TCP windows to maintain throughput. The window extension proposals of RFC 1072 are complementary; together, they address both the throughput problem (via bigger windows) and the reliability problem (via timestamps).
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC solves one specific problem: old data arriving late because the network is fast and fat. Other fixes might be needed for other problems, like windows that are too small to keep the pipe full.
